restatements.text: Titles the act the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026.
Declares findings about the cost of living, taxes, government waste, and the need for transparency and spending limits.
States the purpose is to require the State Auditor to conduct audits of programs receiving new special taxes and to prohibit exemptions from the state spending limit.

Requires the State Auditor to prepare a pre-election financial and performance audit for any proposed special tax initiative, including recommendations for 10% savings, and to publish an executive summary in the voter guide, with costs reimbursed from the tax revenue if passed.
Requires the State Auditor to conduct ongoing audits every four years for programs receiving money from special taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, with costs reimbursed from the tax revenue.
Prohibits any state tax enacted after January 1, 2026, from being exempted from the Government Spending Limitation, and forbids the state from collecting any tax that is exempted.
Defines terms used in the article, including "special tax" and "Government Spending Limitation."

Declares that this measure conflicts with any other measure on the same ballot that imposes different audit rules or exempts a tax from the spending limit, and asserts that this measure prevails if it receives more votes.
Sets the effective date as the earliest possible date allowed by the constitution.
Requires the act to be liberally construed.

Requires the Attorney General to appoint independent counsel to defend the act if the Governor and Attorney General refuse to do so, and creates a continuous appropriation from the General Fund to pay for the counsel.

analysis.answer: Current law was not provided. The measure requires the State Auditor to conduct pre-election and ongoing audits of programs funded by new special taxes. It also prohibits any new state tax from being exempted from the Government Spending Limitation (Gann Limit) and requires the appointment of independent counsel to defend the measure if state officials refuse.

The State Auditor will incur costs to conduct pre-election and ongoing audits. If a special tax initiative passes, these costs are reimbursed from the tax revenue. If an initiative fails, the pre-election audit costs are absorbed by the state. There are also potential costs for retaining independent counsel, funded by a continuous General Fund appropriation.

Taxpayers and voters benefit from increased transparency regarding how special tax revenues will be spent. Programs receiving special tax revenues pay for the audits, as the Auditor's costs are reimbursed from those funds, reducing the money available for the programs themselves.

Initiative proponents might alter how they draft tax measures, potentially favoring general taxes over special taxes to avoid the audit requirements. The state legislature and agencies may face tighter budget constraints if new revenues cannot be exempted from the Gann Limit, potentially forcing tax rebates or increased spending in exempt categories like education.

The text asserts that special taxes are often passed without sufficient transparency and frequently bypass the state's constitutional spending limit. The measure addresses this by mandating detailed audits before and after a special tax is enacted and by constitutionally prohibiting new taxes from being exempted from the spending limit.
The California State Auditor gains significant responsibility and influence over the evaluation of proposed and existing special tax programs.
A portion of the revenue generated by any new special tax will be diverted to reimburse the State Auditor for the administrative costs of conducting the required pre-election and ongoing audits.
Because it amends the California Constitution, it can only be undone or modified by another voter-approved constitutional amendment.

flags.quote: Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 12500) of Part 2 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code or any other law
flags.note: Overrides other laws to ensure the Attorney General appoints independent counsel.
The reimbursement amount for the State Auditor depends on the Controller's determination of reasonable costs.

flags.quote: If the special tax initiative is approved by voters, the California State Auditor shall be reimbursed from the revenue generated by the special tax initiative for reasonable costs incurred
flags.note: If the initiative fails, there is no provision for reimbursing the Auditor for the pre-election audit, creating an unfunded mandate.

flags.quote: The provisions of this Act are severable.
This Act shall take effect at the earliest possible date in accordance with Section 10 of Article II of the California Constitution.
flags.note: Sets the effective date to the earliest possible constitutional date.

flags.quote: require the California State Auditor to conduct upfront and ongoing audits of all state programs that are targeted to receive revenue from new or higher special taxes. The audits must identify areas of potential savings and improvements and the results must be shared with the public in order to ensure that extra funding is actually needed, that public programs are delivering results, and that taxpayer dollars are not being lost to inefficiency, waste, or abuse-while also prohibiting exemptions from the state spending limit
flags.note: Bundles new audit requirements for special taxes with a broad prohibition on exempting any new state taxes from the Government Spending Limitation.
